items.title: Videolaryngoscopy vs. direct laryngoscopy for tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors (VILARE): a pragmatic multicentre randomised trial.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Videolaryngoscopy has been associated with improved glottic visualisation and higher first-attempt tracheal intubation success compared with direct laryngoscopy. However, multicentre evidence evaluating its effectiveness when tracheal intubation is performed by anaesthesia resident doctors in routine practice is limited. METHODS: Adult patients undergoing surgery requiring tracheal intubation were assigned to videolaryngoscopy or direct laryngoscopy for the initial attempt. All tracheal intubations were performed by anaesthesia residents under consultant supervision. The primary outcome was successful tracheal intubation on the first attempt. Secondary outcomes included glottic visualisation; number of tracheal intubation attempts; need for adjunct airway devices; procedural difficulty; and procedural complications. RESULTS: We enrolled 1001 patients and assigned 501 to videolaryngoscopy and 500 patients to direct laryngoscopy. Successful first-attempt tracheal intubation was achieved in 397 (79.2%) patients allocated to the videolaryngoscopy group and 351 (70.2%) patients allocated to the direct laryngoscopy group (absolute risk difference 9.0%, 95%CI 3.7-14.4%, p < 0.001). Videolaryngoscopy improved glottic visualisation, with more patients having a modified Cormack-Lehane grade 2 or 2a view (467/501 (93.3%) vs. 404/500 (80.8%); p < 0.001); decreased operator-reported tracheal intubation difficulty (168/501 (33.5%) vs. 236/500 (47.2%); p < 0.001) and reduced procedural complications (39/501 (7.7%) vs. 91/500 (18.2%); p < 0.001), without a clinically meaningful difference in tracheal intubation time or the need for adjunct airway devices. DISCUSSION: In adult patients undergoing tracheal intubation by anaesthesia resident doctors, videolaryngoscopy increased first-attempt success and improved overall procedural performance compared with direct laryngoscopy. Anaesthesia doctors in training carried out the procedure under the supervision of experienced doctors. items.title: Short-term Modification of Postoperative Ventilation Phenotypes with Electrical Impedance Tomography-guided Positive End-expiratory Pressure Titration.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative ventilation inhomogeneity is common after major surgery and has been associated with adverse outcomes. Whether these ventilation phenotypes can be acutely modified remains unknown. The authors investigated whether electrical impedance tomography (EIT)-guided positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) titration can improve ventilation homogeneity and cardiopulmonary function. METHODS: This prospective, single-center, nonrandomized feasibility study was conducted from August 2024 to June 2025. Sixty mechanically ventilated adults admitted to the intensive care unit after surgery at high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications underwent EIT assessment. Thirty with heterogeneous ventilation patterns (15 phenotype 1: ventral-dominant; 15 phenotype 3: dorsal-dominant) received individualized PEEP titration guided by dorsal fraction of ventilation (DFV) to achieve a homogeneous pattern (phenotype 2: DFV 50 to 59%), whereas 30 with homogeneous ventilation received no protocolized intervention. The primary endpoint was feasibility of achieving homogenization. RESULTS: Immediate phenotype conversion was achieved in 29 of 30 patients (96.7%; 95% CI, 82.8 to 99.9%). At 4 h, 28 of 30 patients (93.3%; 95% CI, 77.9 to 99.2%) remained within the target DFV range. In ventral-dominant patterns (n = 15), PEEP increased from 5 to 9 cm H 2 O; respiratory system compliance increased by 9.2 ml/cm H 2 O (95% CI, 6.1 to 12.3), and Pa o2 /fraction of inspired oxygen increased by 61.9 mmHg (95% CI, 8.6 to 115.2). In dorsal-dominant patterns (n = 15), PEEP decreased from 7 to 3 cm H 2 O; ventral compliance increased by 3.4 ml/cm H 2 O (95% CI, 1.1 to 5.8) without changes in global respiratory system compliance or oxygenation. Individualized PEEP reduced mean pulmonary artery pressure and increased cardiac index. Exploratory comparison showed severe postoperative pulmonary complications occurred in 25% of the interventional cohort and 41% of the historical cohort (absolute risk difference, -15.8% [95% CI, -38.8 to 2.2]; P = 0.17). CONCLUSIONS: Short-term modification of postoperative ventilation phenotypes is feasible with EIT-guided phenotype-directed PEEP titration. This strategy is associated with improved homogeneity and cardiopulmonary function, supporting regional ventilation as a therapeutic target.

items.title: Development and Validation of a Pre-COPD Score to Predict Incident COPD.
items.abstract: RATIONALE: The ability to predict progression from a pre-disease state in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pre-COPD, to overt COPD remains limited. OBJECTIVE: To test the hypothesis that development of COPD can be predicted by characterizing pre-COPD and creating a simple pre-COPD score. METHODS: We identified individuals without airflow obstruction, defined as pre-bronchodilator (BD) forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1)/forced vital capacity (FVC)≥0.70 and ≥lower limit of normal, from the Copenhagen General Population Study (CGPS)(N = 14,506), Copenhagen City Heart Study (CCHS)(N = 8673), and Genetic Epidemiology for COPD (COPDGene) Study(N = 2982). A pre-COPD score was developed in CGPS by assigning 1 point to each of smoking history≥10 pack-years, active smoking, any respiratory symptom, asthma, and pre-BD FEV1/FVC 0.70-0.75, and 4 points for pre-BD FEV1<80% predicted, indicating presence of Preserved Ratio Impaired Spirometry (PRISm), with external validation in CCHS and COPDGene. Participants were followed for 5-10 years for incident COPD, defined as pre-BD FEV1/FVC<0.70 and FEV1<80% predicted. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: During follow-up, COPD developed in 669 individuals (4.6%) in CGPS, 685 (7.9%) in CCHS, and 367 (12%) in COPDGene. In CGPS, 10-year incidence was 1.5% in the low-risk, 9.3% in the intermediate-risk, 24% in the high-risk, and 42% in the very high-risk category. Corresponding 5-year incidences were 3.7%, 7.3%, 12%, and 25% in CCHS, and 4.1%, 5.3%, 13%, and 31% in COPDGene, respectively. The pre-COPD score demonstrated good discrimination with areas under curve of 0.88 in CGPS, 0.76 in CCHS, and 0.81 in COPDGene. The pre-COPD score was also associated with exacerbations. CONCLUSIONS: The pre-COPD score is useful in predicting the onset of COPD with clinically relevant discrimination in three cohorts with different risk profiles.

items.title: Prefrontal hemodynamic fluctuations and functional connectivity during propofol and sevoflurane anesthesia: A functional near-infrared spectroscopy study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measures cortical hemodynamics, yet its ability to characterize anesthesia-related functional changes remains unclear. METHODS: This exploratory secondary analysis used prospectively collected data from 120 female patients undergoing gynecologic laparoscopic surgery under propofol or sevoflurane anesthesia (60 per group). Twenty-channel prefrontal fNIRS recordings covered wakefulness, induction, and maintenance. Deoxygenated hemoglobin-derived amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), functional connectivity (FC), network topology, and within- and cross-state FC similarity were assessed. Support vector machine, logistic regression, and random forest classifiers assessed discrimination between states. RESULTS: During induction, ALFF increased by 89.8% to 202.2% with propofol and 75.2% to 242.0% with sevoflurane across five prefrontal regions (all P < 0.001). During maintenance, mean ALFF was below awake levels, with significant reductions of 20.0% to 40.1% in three regions under sevoflurane (all P ≤ 0.019). Induction-related FC changes were limited and regionally heterogeneous. Regional FC, modularity, and global efficiency showed no significant maintenance-versus-awake differences in either group. Within-state between-subject FC similarity was significantly higher during maintenance than during wakefulness only with sevoflurane (mean difference [MD], 0.110; 95% CI, 0.054 to 0.169; P < 0.001). Cross-state between-subject FC similarity was higher for awake-maintenance than awake-induction comparisons with propofol (MD, 0.072; 95% CI, 0.055 to 0.090) and sevoflurane (MD, 0.144; 95% CI, 0.126 to 0.161; both P < 0.001). Support vector machine classification of induction versus wakefulness yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.75 to 0.90) for propofol and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.78 to 0.91) for sevoflurane; maintenance-versus-awake AUCs were 0.67 (95% CI, 0.58 to 0.75) and 0.76 (95% CI, 0.68 to 0.85). CONCLUSIONS: Prefrontal fNIRS detected widespread induction-related hemodynamic changes, but the present connectivity measures provided limited discrimination between maintenance of anesthesia and wakefulness.

items.title: A Machine Learning-Based Early Warning System for Renal Replacement Therapy in the Intensive Care Unit.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Renal replacement therapy (RRT) is a life-saving intervention for acute kidney injury in the intensive care unit (ICU). The decision to initiate RRT remains highly complex and subjective. Accurate and timely predictions for the need of RRT initiation are crucial components of personalized care. Using time series patient data (vital signs, laboratory findings, medications, ventilator settings, intake/output, risk scores), we aimed to develop machine learning (ML) models for predicting future initiation of RRT. METHODS: Using data from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-III, MIMIC-IV, and Electronic ICU Collaborative Research Database (eICU), we trained and internally validated models using dataset-specific training, validation, and test splits. We externally validated model performance using held-out eICU hospitals excluded from model development and a temporally distinct cohort of ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic period (2020-2022). Models were developed for: (1) screening patients for prediction of the need for RRT after their first 12 hours in the ICU; and (2) real-time dynamic prediction of the likelihood of documented RRT initiation within the next 24 hours. RESULTS: Here, we summarize the results of the ML model aimed at screening patients for early prediction of RRT. In internal validation, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.886-0.906) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.53 (95% CI, 0.496-0.564) in MIMIC-III. Results were similar in MIMIC-IV and eICU. External validation on ICU patients admitted during the coronavirus disease (COVID) period yielded an AUROC of 0.90 (95% CI, 0.894-0.913) and an AUPRC of 0.57 (95% CI, 0.534-0.602). Additional hospital-level external validation across eight individual eICU hospitals showed AUROCs ranging from 0.86 to 0.91 and AUPRCs ranging from 0.35 to 0.52. Accuracy ranged from 0.78 to 0.84 across validation experiments. CONCLUSION: By accurately identifying patients at high risk for RRT initiation, the early prediction ML model could serve as a triage tool to prompt closer nephrology evaluation or optimization of fluid and hemodynamic management before overt renal failure develops.

items.title: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy During Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation as a Marker of Persistent Organ Support Burden and Post-Decannulation Mortality in Adult Cardiovascular Critical Care: A 9-Year Cohort Study.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) use during extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) serves as a clinical marker of persistent organ support burden and is associated with survival to hospital discharge and post-decannulation mortality among patients successfully separated from ECMO. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Tertiary cardiovascular center, 2017-2025. PARTICIPANTS: Adults (n = 1,224) supported with ECMO, of whom 918 (75.0%) had cardiac failure, 245 (20.0%) underwent extracorporeal cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and 1,164 (95.1%) initially received veno‑arterial (V‑A) ECMO. INTERVENTIONS: CRRT use at any point during the ECMO course; patients without CRRT served as the comparator. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The primary outcome was survival to hospital discharge; secondary analysis examined post‑decannulation death in patients successfully separated from ECMO. Primary severity‑adjusted models included age, sex, ECMO indication, intra‑aortic balloon pump use, pre‑ECMO lactate, and log‑transformed vasoactive‑inotropic score. CRRT was used in 519 (42.4%) patients. Survival to discharge was significantly lower with CRRT than without (149/513 [29.0%] v 380/700 [54.3%]; unadjusted odds ratio [OR], 0.34; 95% CI, 0.27-0.44), and the association remained after severity adjustment (adjusted OR, 0.37; 95% CI, 0.28-0.48). Additional sensitivity models adjusting for pre-ECMO Sequential Organ Failure Assessment score (n = 1,056; adjusted OR, 0.38; 95% CI, 0.29-0.50) and pre-ECMO Survival After Veno-Arterial ECMO score in V-A ECMO (n = 1,052; adjusted OR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.27-0.47) confirmed the consistency of this association. Among 676 patients successfully separated from ECMO, post-decannulation death occurred in 80 of 230 (34.8%) with CRRT and 66 of 446 (14.8%) without CRRT (adjusted OR, 2.69; 95% CI, 1.81-3.99). CONCLUSIONS: CRRT use during ECMO marked a high-risk cardiovascular critical care phenotype with greater persistent organ support burden, lower discharge survival, and higher post-decannulation mortality. These associations should be interpreted as prognostic rather than causal; CRRT status may provide pragmatic information for risk stratification after ECMO separation.

items.title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia for Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Postoperative Cognitive Phenotype.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. METHODS: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9 to 11 yr, with or without previous general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. RESULTS: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (chi-square[1] = 0.01; P = 0.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure, 4.47 ± 3.00 yr) and nonexposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: efficient and vulnerable executive control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with slightly higher odds of belonging to the vulnerable profile group (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI; 1.151 to 1.159; P < 0.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, general anesthesia-exposed participants showed higher global-local precedence measures (estimate, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.04 to 1.01; P = 0.036). CONCLUSIONS: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential postoperative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a higher likelihood to belonging to a vulnerable executive control profile, together with greater visuo-spatial global-local precedence.

items.title: Systemic Inflammation in Bronchiectasis: Data from the EMBARC-BRIDGE Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neutrophilic inflammation in the airways is associated with exacerbation risk in patients with bronchiectasis. Systemic inflammation and neutrophil function are less characterised. The aim of this study was to investigate the relationship between systemic inflammation and neutrophil function with severity of disease and clinical outcomes. METHODS: Observational international multi-centre study of adults with bronchiectasis (EMBARC-BRIDGE). Serum inflammatory profiling was performed in 487 patients using Olink® proteomics, and associations with key clinical and patient reported outcomes, including severe exacerbations during follow-up, were analysed. In a sub-study, peripheral blood neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients and controls were analysed for surface activation and functional markers, and functional responses including degranulation and neutrophil extracellular trap formation. RESULTS: Systemic inflammatory profiling revealed a dominant neutrophil-endothelial signature. Several proteins including PR3, AZU1, MPO, the soluble IL-33 receptor ST2, and the cellular stress marker GDF-15 were associated with increased disease severity using the bronchiectasis severity index, lower lung function, increased symptoms and for many markers, higher rates of severe exacerbations during follow-up. Neutrophils from bronchiectasis patients exhibited reduced surface CD11b and increased CXCR2, with lower CD11b correlating with lower lung function. Basal degranulation was reduced in bronchiectasis, whereas responsiveness to LPS stimulation was preserved. CONCLUSION: Bronchiectasis is associated with a systemic neutrophil and endothelial inflammatory signature linked to disease severity and risk of severe exacerbations, alongside altered but functionally-responsive circulating neutrophils.

items.title: Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. METHODS: We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. RESULTS: Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. DISCUSSION: There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique. We focused on parts of the technique where doctors disagree or where there is not enough good research. items.title: Opioid-free vs. opioid-inclusive anaesthesia in laparoscopic cholecystectomy: a multicentre randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the most common abdominal operation worldwide, yet whether opioid-free anaesthesia improves the overall analgesic benefit remains uncertain. METHODS: In this multicentre randomised controlled trial, adults undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy were randomised 1:1 to receive opioid-free anaesthesia (dexmedetomidine, esketamine and sevoflurane) or opioid-inclusive anaesthesia (sufentanil and sevoflurane). Patients received prophylactic anti-emetics and multimodal analgesia with flurbiprofen axetil and ropivacaine wound infiltration. The primary outcome was the overall benefit of analgesia score (0-28, lower scores indicate greater benefit) at 24 h postoperatively; a 3-point difference was considered clinically relevant. Secondary outcomes included pain on movement at 24 h and chronic postsurgical pain at 90 days. RESULTS: Between March and September 2025, 315 patients completed this trial (158 opioid-free, 157 opioid-inclusive). The mean (SD) 24-h overall benefit of analgesia score was 2.2 (2.4) after opioid-free anaesthesia vs 3.4 (3.1) after opioid-inclusive anaesthesia (adjusted mean difference -1.3; 95%CI -1.8 to -0.8, p < 0.001), without reaching the threshold for clinical importance. Incidence of pain on movement (adjusted mean difference -0.2; 95%CI -0.4-0) and chronic postsurgical pain (16.1% vs 15.5%; adjusted relative risk 1.03; 95%CI 0.55-1.91) did not differ between groups. Opioid-free anaesthesia was associated with reduced intra-operative hypotension (19.6% vs 35.7%; relative risk 0.55; 95%CI 0.37-0.80) and lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (23.4% vs 33.8%; relative risk 0.69; 95%CI 0.48-0.98). DISCUSSION: Opioid-free anaesthesia did not achieve a clinically meaningful improvement in overall benefit of analgesia. These findings do not support its routine adoption in laparoscopic cholecystectomy. However, the observed reductions in intra-operative hypotension and postoperative nausea and vomiting suggest that this regimen may warrant consideration in selected patients, pending validation in future trials. items.title: Erector Spinae Plane Block Versus Serratus Anterior Plane Block in Minimally Invasive Cardiac Surgery Via Minithoracotomy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: The aim of this study was to compare the efficacy of 2 regional anesthesia techniques- erector spinae plane (ESP) block and serratus anterior plane (SAP) block-for cardiac surgery with a minithoracotomy approach. The primary outcome was postoperative quality of recovery assessed using the Italian Quality of Recovery questionnaire (iQoR-15) on postoperative days 1 and 2. Secondary outcomes included static and dynamic pain scores, morphine consumption, and complications. DESIGN: Randomized controlled trial. SETTING: Community hospital center. PARTICIPANTS: Patients underwent minimally invasive cardiac surgery with minithoracotomy approach. INTERVENTIONS: Patients were randomized 1:1 to receive either ESP or SAP block preoperatively with ropivacaine 0.5% (30 mL) plus dexmedetomidine (1 µg/kg), followed by a second postoperative block on day 1 without adjuvant. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Fifty-seven patients were analyzed (ESP n = 28; SAP n = 29) with comparable baseline and surgical characteristics. iQoR-15 scores improved significantly from days 1 to 2 in both groups, with no statistically significant intergroup differences; static and dynamic Numerical Rating Scale pain scores were significantly lower in the SAP group during the first 48 hours (p < 0.05). Total morphine consumption was similar between groups (ESP 22 mg [10-33 mg] v SAP 14 mg [8-36 mg]; p = 0.5). One episode of local anesthetic systemic toxicity occurred in the ESP group; no additional major complications were observed. CONCLUSIONS: The SAP block provided comparable recovery quality and superior pain control compared with ESP block, with equivalent opioid consumption. Its technical simplicity and favorable safety profile support the SAP block as a practical component of ERACS multimodal analgesia strategies.

items.title: Surgical wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine for post-caesarean analgesia: a randomised, double-blind controlled trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrathecal morphine is the gold standard for post-caesarean analgesia, but it lasts only 18-24 h. Whether wound infiltration adds benefit in patients receiving intrathecal morphine remains controversial. This study evaluated the opioid-sparing efficacy of wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine. METHODS: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 188 patients undergoing elective caesarean delivery with intrathecal morphine (100 μg) received either wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine (266 mg) plus bupivacaine hydrochloride (100 mg), or saline placebo. All patients received standardised multimodal analgesia including scheduled non-opioid analgesics and hydromorphone patient-controlled analgesia. The primary outcome was cumulative opioid consumption (oral morphine milligram equivalents) at 48 h. RESULTS: With treatment, 48-h opioid consumption was significantly lower (12.60 mg [IQR 6.30-15.80] vs. 15.75 mg [IQR 9.45-25.50]; Hodges-Lehmann estimate -3.05 mg, 95% CI -5.9 to -1.4; P = 0.002). Secondary outcomes also favoured treatment: 24-h opioid consumption (6.30 vs. 9.45 mg; P < 0.001), movement-evoked pain at 24 h (40 vs. 50 mm; P < 0.001) and 48 h (30 vs. 40 mm; P < 0.001), time to first analgesic request (14.5 vs. 9.5 h; P < 0.001), and opioid-free status at 48 h (19.1% vs. 2.1%; RR 9.0; 95% CI 2.1-37.8; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In women undergoing scheduled caesarean delivery, wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture significantly reduced postoperative opioid consumption and improved pain scores. It may be an effective opioid-sparing adjunct to intrathecal morphine.

items.title: Incidence of pain, supplemental analgesia and conversion to general anaesthesia during intrapartum caesarean delivery using converted epidural anaesthesia: a meta-analysis.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: It is common practice to convert an existing labour epidural into surgical anaesthesia for intrapartum caesarean delivery. However, this approach does not always provide adequate anaesthesia. This meta-analysis aimed to determine the incidence of inadequate anaesthesia during epidural conversion for intrapartum caesarean delivery. METHODS: Databases were searched for observational studies and randomised controlled trials evaluating epidural conversion for intrapartum caesarean delivery. Using a random-effects model and the Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation, we calculated the respective incidences of intra-operative patient-reported pain; use of supplemental analgesia; and conversion to general anaesthesia. RESULTS: A total of 43 studies, involving 11,904 patients, were included in the meta-analysis. Pooled incidences of intra-operative pain (eight studies), supplemental analgesia (34 studies) and conversion to general anaesthesia (33 studies) were 20.2% (95%CI 12.2-29.5%, I2 = 93.1%), 17.7% (95%CI 13.3-22.7%, I2 = 96.3%) and 1.3% (95%CI 0.7-2.1%, I2 = 81.7%), respectively. These results were consistent in sensitivity analyses and appeared unaffected by publication year, study design, country type, local anaesthetic used or use of epidural fentanyl. However, substantial heterogeneity was observed due to variability in study methodologies, measurement methods, definitions, thresholds and local clinical practices. DISCUSSION: This meta-analysis highlights the risk of inadequate anaesthesia and emphasises the importance of thorough pre-operative informed consent when converting labour epidurals to surgical anaesthesia for intrapartum caesarean delivery. However, the considerable heterogeneity in the pooled estimates indicates that these incidences vary significantly across different settings, suggesting that local audit data would be more informative for individual practices. WHAT WE DID: We reviewed 43 studies involving almost 12,000 women who needed a caesarean birth during labour. We looked at how often an epidural that had been used for labour did not provide enough pain relief when it was used to provide anaesthesia for the operation. WHY WE DID IT: An epidural can help relieve pain during labour. If a woman needs a caesarean birth, doctors may use the same epidural to provide anaesthesia for the operation. However, it does not always work well enough. We wanted to find out how often women experience pain or need extra pain relief

items.title: Effect of Wrist Extension Angle on Radial and Ulnar Artery Sonoanatomy in Children: A Prospective Ultrasound Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided radial artery cannulation is common in pediatrics but technically challenging. While the ulnar artery is a potential alternative, its sonoanatomy relative to the radial artery is not well defined. AIMS: This study aimed to compare the sonoanatomic characteristics of the radial and ulnar arteries in children, evaluating how age, weight, and wrist position (0°, 30°, and 45°) influence arterial dimensions and depth to identify the most favorable profile for cannulation. METHODS: Ultrasound evaluation of the radial and ulnar arteries was performed at 0°, 30°, and 45° wrist extension in 180 anesthetized children aged 0-120 months using custom-made wooden blocks. Arterial dimensions and skin-to-artery distance were evaluated overall and across age (≤ 24 vs. > 24 months) and weight (≤ 12 vs. > 12 kg) subgroups to identify optimal access conditions. RESULTS: Wrist extension angle did not significantly affect anteroposterior diameter (1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.078), but significantly influenced transverse arterial diameter (1.5-1.6 mm, p = 0.003) and skin-to-artery distance (2.4-2.8 mm at 30°, p < 0.001). The radial artery was widest at 0° (1.6 ± 1.0 mm), while the ulnar artery peaked at 30° (1.6 ± 0.4 mm). Skin-to-artery distance was minimized at 30° for both vessels. In children ≤ 12 kg, radial transverse diameter decreased paradoxically from 0° to 45° (1.6 ± 0.4 to 1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.013), while the ulnar artery was widest at 30° (1.5 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.007). In infants ≤ 24 months, wrist angle did not significantly influence radial artery depth (p = 0.631, mean overall depth between 2.5-2.6 mm). CONCLUSION: A 30° wrist extension angle provides the most favorable sonoanatomic profile for both arteries. Although a larger vessel caliber may potentially facilitate cannulation, its clinical benefit remains uncertain as cannulation outcomes were not assessed. These findings support individualized ultrasound-guided assessment rather than a fixed positioning strategy.

items.title: Disparities in Regional Analgesia Utilization for Rib Fractures: Hospital-Level Variation, Trends, and Clinical Outcomes in a Nationwide Retrospective Cohort Study 2016 to 2022.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Regional analgesia is recommended for rib fractures, but utilization remains low. The extent to which hospital-level factors drive utilization and influence patient outcomes is unclear. This study's objective was to evaluate associations between hospital characteristics and regional analgesia receipt and outcomes. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample (NIS) of adult hospitalizations (>18 years) between January 1, 2016, and December 31, 2022 with rib fractures. Exposures included hospital bed-size, ownership, teaching status and geographic region. Primary outcome was regional analgesia receipt. Secondary outcomes included in-hospital mortality and tracheostomy. RESULTS: 250,630 hospitalizations met inclusion criteria, of which 7,179 (2.9%) received regional analgesia. After adjustment, 23.9% of variation in utilization was attributable to between-hospital differences. Greater utilization was associated with large hospital bed-size (odds ratio [OR] 2.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.80-2.39), urban teaching-status (OR 1.39; 95% CI, 1.19-1.62), higher income-quartile (OR 1.21; 95% CI, 1.10-1.33), and private insurance (OR 1.24; 95% CI, 1.14-1.35). Lower odds were observed in private nonprofit (OR 0.75; 95% CI, 0.65-0.86) and for-profit hospitals (OR 0.42; 95% CI, 0.34-0.53) compared with government hospitals. Regional analgesia utilization varied geographically, with the highest utilization in New England. Private insurance, White race, highest income quartile, government ownership and urban teaching status were also associated with earlier receipt of regional anesthesia. Disparities by insurance and hospital characteristics either persisted or widened from 2016 to 2022.Regional analgesia was associated with lower mortality (OR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.42-0.64) and tracheostomy (OR, 0.48; 95% CI, 0.36-0.63) in multivariable analysis. In instrumental variable analysis with leave-one-out hospital-year regional analgesia rate as the instrument, these associations were attenuated. CONCLUSIONS: Regional analgesia remains infrequently utilized for rib fractures, with marked variation across hospitals. Access and outcomes appear to depend substantially on where patients receive care. Understanding the institutional and provider-level factors underlying this variation represents an important target for future quality-improvement and implementation efforts.

items.title: Quadratus lumborum block with or without subfascial wound catheter and post-caesarean delivery pain outcomes: a single-center retrospective cohort study (2026).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: We evaluated whether adding a subfascial wound catheter to a posterior quadratus lumborum block-based multimodal analgesic pathway improves pain and recovery after caesarean delivery. METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 361 women undergoing scheduled or urgent caesarean delivery from January to June 2026. All received bilateral posterior quadratus lumborum block and non-opioid multimodal analgesia; wound catheter use was optional. Ropivacaine infusion was continued for 48 h. Pain scores were recorded at 6, 24, and 48 h. Mobilisation, rescue analgesia, satisfaction, breastfeeding-related concern, breastfeeding outcomes, and repeat quadratus lumborum block were assessed. Catheter effects on pain were analysed using generalized estimating equations adjusted for anaesthetic technique, operative duration, repeat caesarean delivery, adhesions, age, and blood loss. RESULTS: Catheter use was associated with lower pain scores at 6 h (adjusted difference - 0.209, 95% confidence interval - 0.369 to -0.049; P = 0.011) and 24 h (-0.174, -0.309 to -0.039; P = 0.012), but not at 48 h (-0.016, -0.139 to 0.108; P = 0.805). These differences were too small to be clinically meaningful. Mobilisation, rescue analgesia, satisfaction, and breastfeeding outcomes were similar between groups. Breastfeeding-related concern was greater with catheter use. Repeat quadratus lumborum block was infrequently required and did not delay return to normal activity. DISCUSSION: Subfascial wound catheter use was not associated with clinically meaningful additional pain or recovery benefit. Patient counselling may help address breastfeeding-related concerns.

items.title: Rethinking the Responsible Adult Requirement after Ambulatory Anesthesia: Toward Risk-stratified Discharge.
items.abstract: For decades, ambulatory anesthesia pathways have commonly required a "responsible adult" before discharge after sedation or anesthesia. In practice, this requirement may function as a binary eligibility criterion based on a patient's social circumstances. However, the empirical evidence evaluating discharge without an escort remains limited and derives largely from observational studies. This Focal Point argues that carefully selected low-risk patients should be studied within structured alternative discharge pathways that preserve safe transportation, communication, observation, and rescue capacity. Such pathways should not permit self-driving or unrestricted solo discharge. The aim is to determine whether postanesthesia safeguards can be matched more precisely to patient, anesthetic, procedural, recovery, transport, and postdischarge risk while preserving conventional adult support for patients whose clinical circumstances warrant it.

items.title: Receipt of Extended-release Opioids after Total Hip or Knee Arthroplasty and Subsequent Persistent Postoperative Opioid Use and Health System Utilization: A Population-based Comparative Effectiveness Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Extended-release opioids (EROs), continue to be used for acute pain after surgery despite guideline recommendations discouraging their use. This study examined the association of filling a new postoperative ERO prescription with persistent postoperative opioid use (PPOU), clinical events, and health system outcomes among patients undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty. METHODS: A population-based comparative effectiveness study of adult residents of Ontario, Canada, undergoing elective primary total hip or knee arthroplasty between 2013 and 2022 was conducted. Linked administrative data sets were used to identify patients who filled an ERO prescription within 7 days of discharge. The primary outcome was PPOU, defined using a measure accounting for preoperative opioid exposure (opioid naïve, exposed, tolerant [O-NET]). Secondary outcomes included rates of 90-day readmissions, 90-day emergency department visits, the number of days alive at home in the first year, and 365-day total health system costs. Associations were estimated using propensity score overlap weighting to balance demographic, clinical, and perioperative covariates. RESULTS: Among 258,624 patients, 31,224 (12.1%) filled a new postoperative ERO prescription. Among those who filled an ERO prescription, 1,860 (6.0%) developed PPOU, compared to 11,804 (5.2%) without ERO. After weighting, filling an ERO prescription was associated with increased odds of PPOU (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.08; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.15), higher 90-day readmissions (aOR, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.02 to 1.17), and emergency department visits (aOR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.21). In contrast, total health system costs were lower (ratio of means, 0.87; 95% CI, 0.85 to 0.89) and days alive at home were higher (ratio of means, 1.002; 95% CI, 1.0004 to 1.003) at 365 days. CONCLUSIONS: Using O-NET criteria, 6% of patients receiving new postoperative ERO prescriptions develop PPOU. Filling a new ERO prescription was associated with small but consistent increases in adverse clinical outcomes balanced against decreased 1-yr health system costs. Combined with concerns regarding opioid-related harm and the opioid epidemic, these findings reinforce a cautious approach in postoperative ERO prescribing.

items.title: Patient-reported outcomes, postoperative pain and pain relief after day-case surgery (POPPY): persistent postoperative opioid use prevalence and associations.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: An increasing proportion of complex surgical procedures are being performed in the UK as day-cases, and NHS targets aim for these to encompass ≥ 75% of all surgeries. There has been limited outcome follow-up for this group of patients, particularly considering the prevalence of persistent postoperative opioid use and factors associated with its occurrence. METHODS: Data from POPPY, a national, prospective, observational study exploring outcomes following day-case surgery in the UK, were used to estimate the prevalence of persistent postoperative opioid use at day 97 following surgery. Patient, anaesthetic and surgical factors associated with increased persistent postoperative opioid use were explored using multivariable analysis. RESULTS: Of the 7839 initially recruited patients, 3488 (44.5%) provided details of their analgesic medication at day 97 following surgery. The prevalence of daily persistent postoperative opioid use was estimated to be 11.8% (95%CI 11.1-13.2%). Patient factors associated with daily persistent postoperative opioid use were pre-operative opioid use; opioid use at day 7; and composite pain scores (day 1, day 3 and day 7). Compared with general surgery, ENT, breast and orthopaedic surgery carried a higher risk of persistent postoperative opioid use. Patient factors associated with a reduced odds ratio of persistent postoperative opioid use were: female sex; higher composite pain score at baseline; and Index of Multiple Deprivation quintile 4. Daily persistent postoperative opioid use at day 97 following surgery was associated with reduced quality of life scores. DISCUSSION: Daily persistent postoperative opioid use is common in the UK following day-case surgery. Patient and surgical factors that are associated with an increased risk of this outcome could be used to drive improvement in identification of at-risk patients pre-operatively and optimise postoperative prescribing pathways. We wanted to find out how many people were still taking opioid medicines for pain relief every day about three months after their operation. items.title: Regional Anesthesia for Outpatient Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator Implantation:A 5-Year Retrospective Study.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate whether regional anesthesia (RA) facilitates same-day discharge after outpatient subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) implantation. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Two quaternary-care academic medical centers. PARTICIPANTS: Outpatients undergoing S-ICD implantation from January 2020 to December 2024. INTERVENTIONS: Baseline demographic characteristics, perioperative variables, and outcomes were abstracted from the electronic health record. Univariate comparisons were made between patients who received RA and those who did not receive RA. Additionally, a multivariable logistic regression model estimated independent associations for same-day discharge. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: Of the 143 included outpatients, 63 received RA (RA group) and 80 did not receive RA (no RA group). Same-day discharge occurred more often in the RA group than in the no RA group (45 [71%] v 36 [45%], p = 0.002). Patients who received RA needed fewer airway interventions such as supraglottic airway or endotracheal intubation (13 [20.6%] v 70 [87.5%], p < 0.001), had lower intraprocedural heart rate (HR) variability (median difference between maximum and minimum intraoperative HR [interquartile range (IQR)], 25 bpm [18-33] v 40 bpm [27-48]; p < 0.001), had lower mean arterial pressure (MAP) variability (mean difference between maximum and minimum intraoperative MAP [95% confidence interval (CI)], 41.1 mm Hg [11.9-30.3] v 45.6 mm Hg [10.4-81]; p = 0.07)], and required less vasopressor administration (34 patients v 71 patients, p < 0.001). After the procedure, the RA group had a shorter recovery time (235 minutes v 284 minutes, p = 0.016) and lower postoperative opioid requirements (median [IQR], 0 mg [0-10 mg] v 7.5 mg [0-22.5 mg]; p = 0.003). In multivariable logistic regression analysis, RA was associated with higher odds of same-day discharge (adjusted odds ratio, 3.27; 95% CI, 1.07-9.73) whereas advancing age and afternoon start time were associated with lower odds of same-day discharge. CONCLUSIONS: In outpatient S-ICD implantation, RA was associated with a higher likelihood of same-day discharge, lower periprocedural opioid requirements, reduced intraprocedural vasopressor use, and less HR variability. These findings suggest that RA may support perioperative efficiency in selected patients undergoing outpatient S-ICD implantation.

items.title: Management of breakthrough pain during advanced labor with epidural alkalinized lidocaine 0.3%-epinephrine: a single-center retrospective study (2022-2026).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Breakthrough pain during advanced labor requires rapid analgesia while limiting motor block. We describe responses to epidural alkalinized lidocaine 0.3% with epinephrine 10 µg/mL. METHODS: This single-center retrospective cohort included women receiving epidural alkalinized lidocaine 0.3%-epinephrine for breakthrough pain at cervical dilation of at least 7 cm after satisfactory neuraxial analgesia. Women with recurrent epidural boluses suggesting catheter dysfunction were excluded. Median bolus volume was 3 mL [interquartile range, 3-5]. The primary outcome was contraction-pain visual analog scale change from baseline to 5-15 min. Secondary outcomes included sensory and motor changes. Brackets indicate interquartile ranges. Paired assessments preceded delivery. RESULTS: Of 153 women, 143 were analyzed. Median visual analog scale decreased from 50 [30-60] to 0 [0-0] mm (mean reduction, 45.2; 95% confidence interval, 41.9-48.4); 126 (88.1%) scored 10 mm or less. Median rescue-to-delivery interval was 52 min [31-88]. Median cephalad cold-loss extension was one dermatome [1-2]. Modified Bromage scores were unchanged in 138 (96.5%) and worsened in five (3.5%). Maternal hypotension and new fetal heart rate abnormalities each affected six women (4.2%). Among vaginal deliveries, operative delivery rates were 9.3 and 0.6 percentage points higher in nulliparous and parous women, respectively, than in same-period deliveries with neuraxial analgesia without the study rescue. DISCUSSION: Epidural alkalinized lidocaine 0.3%-epinephrine (3-8 mL) was followed by early pain reduction with infrequent motor block increase, supporting clinical application of prior laboratory findings. Prospective comparisons should assess motor function and delivery outcomes.

items.title: Sugammadex interference with serum progesterone measurement: an in-vitro study.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Sugammadex may interfere with serum progesterone immunoassays, potentially rendering measured concentrations and resulting recommendations unreliable. METHODS: We investigated the effect of a range of sugammadex concentrations on serum progesterone concentrations in samples from pre-menopausal female volunteers. Samples were spiked with sugammadex concentrations (15-120 μM), corresponding to clinical doses between 2 mg.kg-1 and 19 mg.kg-1. Total progesterone concentrations in each sample were determined using the routine electrochemiluminescence immunoassay method. A subgroup of 15 samples underwent further testing using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy, comparing baseline with sugammadex 120 μM. RESULTS: Thirty-five participants provided blood samples. Increasing concentrations of sugammadex were associated with lower measured serum progesterone, with an approximate 10% reduction with each doubling of sugammadex concentration (F(2,30) = 4.86, p = 0.015). Overall, progesterone concentrations decreased by a mean (SD) of 34.6% (12.4%) between control samples and those spiked with sugammadex 120 μM (p = 0.015). In contrast, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy showed no statistically significant biochemical change in progesterone concentrations between baseline and sugammadex 120 μM. DISCUSSION: Sugammadex produced a dose-dependent reduction in the progesterone concentrations when measured by immunoassay techniques, but not by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectroscopy. This suggests that an immunoassay interference occurs across clinically relevant doses. Progesterone results from routine laboratory testing should be interpreted with caution in the presence of sugammadex. We added different amounts of sugammadex to the samples and then measured progesterone levels using a common hospital laboratory test. We also checked some samples using a second, more precise testing method. There were concerns that sugammadex, a medicine often used after anaesthesia, might interfere with progesterone blood tests and make the results inaccurate. We wanted to find out if this was true.
