items.title: Causes of bias in Delphi studies and consensus statements: a methodological review.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: The Delphi methodology is a widely-used tool for achieving expert consensus in healthcare, particularly in areas where empirical evidence is limited or uncertain. Despite its structured design, the Delphi process remains vulnerable to implicit cognitive biases that may influence judgement and group decision-making. Such biases may inadvertently affect the quality of the consensus process, allow louder voices to influence outcomes, restrict inclusivity and undermine the validity, transparency and evidence-based nature of recommendations. METHODS: We conducted a methodological review synthesising literature from cognitive psychology, behavioural science and methodological research on consensus development and Delphi processes. Using a concept-mapping approach, established cognitive biases were mapped to different stages of the Delphi process, including study design; panel selection; survey development; iterative scoring; and consensus interpretation. RESULTS: Ten cognitive biases were organised into four domains reflecting different levels of influence within consensus development: steering-group and design-level biases, panel composition and contextual biases, social influence and conformity biases; and individual cognitive heuristic biases. A conceptual framework was developed to systematically identify these biases within Delphi-based consensus studies. Examples illustrating how these biases may arise in healthcare Delphi processes are presented, alongside potential mitigation strategies. DISCUSSION: Recognition and mitigation of cognitive biases are essential for strengthening the methodological rigour and credibility of Delphi studies. Strategies to reduce bias include diversifying expert panels; using neutral language in survey statements; maintaining anonymity during voting; involving methodological expertise in Delphi design; and ensuring transparent iterative feedback. The framework needs prospective validation before its widespread use and may assist journal editors and peer reviewers in critically appraising Delphi studies and improving reporting standards in consensus research. We brought together ideas from psychology and research methods to find ways that hidden thinking mistakes, called biases, might affect each stage of a Delphi study. items.title: Rapid sequence induction: a narrative review.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pulmonary aspiration of gastric contents remains an important cause of anaesthetic morbidity and mortality, and is important medicolegally. Rapid sequence induction is a multi-element technique designed to mitigate risk in those patients at increased risk of pulmonary aspiration during induction of general anaesthesia. METHODS: We undertook a narrative review to summarise evidence and evidence gaps focusing on controversial aspects of rapid sequence induction. RESULTS: Despite widespread use of rapid sequence induction, many elements of the technique lack robust evidence and consensus. Nasogastric tubes can be used to reduce gastric content, but do not empty the stomach reliably. Correctly applied cricoid force obstructs the hypopharynx and has a limited impact on airway management, but incorrect application can cause clinically significant difficulties. Correct location of cricoid force may require ultrasound localisation of the cricoid cartilage. Applying the correct force, which varies with age and sex, is improved by education, practice and feedback. The use of videolaryngoscopy during rapid sequence induction is supported by evidence. The role of gastric ultrasound in determining anaesthetic technique is uncertain. Cardiovascular complications of rapid sequence induction are common, particularly in the patients who are critically ill, and modifications to the technique may reduce their frequency and severity. Effective use of airway rescue techniques may require removal of cricoid force. DISCUSSION: There is insufficient evidence for many of the elements of rapid sequence induction to determine whether they reduce patient harm or to state confidently that they do not. Controversies and evidence gaps should be acknowledged. Despite this, optimal use of rapid sequence induction requires a thorough knowledge of the subject, including areas of uncertainty to guide individualised risk assessment; clinical decision-making; and practical conduct of the technique. items.title: Volume Guarantee Versus Manual Tidal Volume Monitoring During High-Frequency Oscillatory Ventilation in Neonates: A Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The present study compared the effects of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (HFOV) with automated volume guarantee (HFOV-VG) versus careful manual high-frequency tidal volume (VThf) monitoring (HFOV-VM) on the incidences of hypo/hypercarbia in neonates. METHODS: In this open-labeled, parallel-group randomized controlled trial, 60 neonates failing conventional mechanical ventilation were allocated to receive HFOV-VG (n = 30) versus HFOV-VM (n = 30) as a rescue mode. The primary outcome was the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia at 1 h. Secondary outcomes were incidences of hypo/hypercarbia at 6/12/24/48 h and beyond, time-specific trends for partial pressure of carbon dioxide (pCO2), delivered VThf and mean airway pressure (MAP), cerebral blood flow (CBF) in the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and regional cerebral oxygenation (CrSO2), duration of respiratory support, and incidences of in-hospital adverse events. Stata 18 was used for an intention-to-treat analysis. RESULTS: The incidence of hypo- or hypercarbia at 1 h of intervention was 15/30 (50%) in the HFOV-VG and 13/30 (43%) in the HFOV-VM groups (p = 0.61). No differences were observed in the incidences of hypo- or hypercarbia anytime during HFOV. Time-specific pCO2, VThf, and MAP were similar. On regression analysis, the only significant predictor for pCO2 at 1 h was the baseline pCO2 level in both the groups. No difference was observed in ACA-CBF, CrSO2, duration of respiratory support, and in-hospital adverse events including mortality. CONCLUSION: There was no difference in the incidence of hypo/hypercarbia with HFOV-VG versus HFOV-VM at 1 h and throughout the duration of ventilation with a similar rate of complications when used as a rescue therapy. items.title: Preoperative Oral Esketamine for Perioperative Comfort in Children Undergoing Adenotonsillectomy: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Dose-Finding Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pediatric adenotonsillectomy often causes preoperative anxiety, venous cannulation pain, and emergence agitation. Esketamine has multimodal properties, but the optimal oral dose for children is unknown. This study evaluated oral esketamine at 1, 2, and 3 mg/kg for perioperative comfort. METHODS: In this randomized double-blind trial, 99 children (ASA I-II, 1-6 years) received oral 10% glucose (control, n = 26) or esketamine 1 mg/kg (EK1, n = 26), 2 mg/kg (EK2, n = 23), or 3 mg/kg (EK3, n = 24) 30 min before anesthesia. PRIMARY OUTCOMES: Ramsay Sedation Scale (RSS) and FLACC pain score at venous cannulation, and PAED score at 15 min after extubation. SECONDARY OUTCOMES: remifentanil use, postoperative FLACC (2-48 h), sleep quality, and adverse events. RESULTS: All esketamine doses improved sedation and analgesia at cannulation (overall p < 0.001), with largest effect at 3 mg/kg. Median RSS (IQR): control 1.00 (1.00-2.00); EK1 2.00 (1.75-3.00, p = 0.028); EK2 2.00 (1.00-3.00, p = 0.049); EK3 3.00 (2.00-3.37, p < 0.001). FLACC scores: control 6.00 (3.00-7.00); EK1 2.50 (1.00-4.00, p = 0.016); EK2 2.00 (0.00-4.00, p = 0.001); EK3 0.00 (0.00-1.75, p < 0.001). PAED score at 15 min was lower in EK2 than control (5.00 [2.00-10.00] vs. 10.00 [6.00-12.00], p = 0.048). Remifentanil consumption was reduced in EK3 (120.00 [80.00-159.50] vs. 240.00 [160.00-315.00] μg, p = 0.001). Postoperative pain at 2-6 h was lower in EK2 and EK3 (p < 0.05), persisting to 48 h in EK3 (p < 0.05). Sleep quality improved in EK3 at 24 h (p = 0.023) and 48 h (p = 0.032). Adverse events did not differ significantly. CONCLUSIONS: Preoperative oral esketamine (1-3 mg/kg) enhances perioperative comfort in children undergoing adenotonsillectomy. The 2 mg/kg dose offers the best balance of efficacy and safety, while 3 mg/kg provides superior analgesia and opioid sparing.

items.title: EEG-Guided Sevoflurane Anesthesia and Emergence Delirium in Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: In pediatric anesthesia, minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) guides inhalational agent dosing but may not accurately reflect anesthetic depth. EEG-guided anesthesia has shown benefits in adults but remains underused in children. AIMS: This study aims to evaluate the effect of EEG-guided anesthesia with SedLine on emergence delirium (ED) and sevoflurane dose in behaviorally noncompliant children undergoing dental procedures under general anesthesia. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized controlled trial, 100 children aged 4-10 years were randomized to standard anesthesia guided by MAC and conventional clinical signs (standard group) or EEG-guided anesthesia titrated to SedLine parameters (primary target: PSI 25-50; secondary parameter: SEF 10-15 Hz) (EEG-S group). Primary outcome was ED incidence assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium Scale (PAEDS). Secondary outcomes included mean EtSevo values, postoperative pain, rescue analgesia, nausea/vomiting, recovery time. RESULTS: Median PAEDS scores during the first 120 min postoperatively were significantly lower in the EEG-S group compared with the Standard group (e.g., upon arrival to PACU: 4 [IQR 4] vs. 8 [IQR 4.5]). In addition, the incidence of ED upon arrival in the recovery room was significantly lower in the EEG-S group (17% vs. 43%) and at 10 min postoperatively (17% vs. 37%). The mean end-tidal sevoflurane concentration was statistically lower in the EEG-S group (maintenance EtSevo 1.88 ± 0.25 vs. 1.98 ± 0.20; mean difference = 0.10, 95% confidence interval: 0.006-0.190; p = 0.036). Postoperative FLACC pain scores were also lower in the EEG-S group, representing a potential confounding factor for ED outcomes. CONCLUSION: EEG-guided anesthesia was associated with lower PAEDS scores and reduced sevoflurane consumption compared with standard management. However, given small EEG-derived differences and potential confounding by postoperative pain, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Within the applied target ranges, EEG-derived parameters were not independently associated with ED, and specific EEG targets predictive of ED could not be identified. TRIAL REGISTRATION: This study was registered (Protocol Registration Receipt NCT06400706/OKocaturk/May 02 2024) at http://www. CLINICALTRIAL: gov.

items.title: Intraoperative active warming with or without active prewarming on maternal hypothermia in patients undergoing elective cesarean delivery with spinal anesthesia: A randomized controlled study.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Maternal hypothermia affects up to 60% of patients undergoing scheduled cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia and is associated with maternal and neonatal morbidity. Although intraoperative active warming is standard, the effect of preoperative warming to improve zero-flux core temperature remains unclear. METHODS: In this randomized clinical trial, 78 women scheduled for cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia received intraoperative forced-air warming and warmed crystalloids. The active group received 20 min of preoperative forced-air warming. The primary outcome was zero-flux core maternal temperature on arrival to post-anesthesia care unit. Secondary maternal outcomes included intraoperative shivering and in post-anesthesia care unit, maternal hypothermia (core temperature < 36 °C), thermal comfort scores in post-anesthesia care unit, and neonatal temperature. The Mann-Whitney U test and the Chi-Square test were used for analysis. RESULTS: Median with interquartile range [IQR] core temperature on arrival to post-anesthesia care unit did not differ between the active and control groups (36.6 °C [36.45-36.85] vs. 36.6 °C [36-36.75]; P = 0.99). Hypothermia incidence was 5.1% in the active group vs. 15.4% in the control group (P = 0.161). Shivering incidence was 10.3% in the active group vs. 28.2% in the control group (P = 0.06). Thermal comfort scores were significantly higher in the active warming group (52.05 ± 6.56 vs. 43.84 ± 10.91; P = 0.0001). CONCLUSION: Adding 20 min of preoperative forced-air warming to active intraoperative warming did not significantly increase core temperature or reduce hypothermia upon arrival to post-anesthesia care unit. However, active pre-warming significantly improved maternal thermal comfort.

items.title: Surgical wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine for post-caesarean analgesia: a randomised, double-blind controlled trial.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrathecal morphine is the gold standard for post-caesarean analgesia, but it lasts only 18-24 h. Whether wound infiltration adds benefit in patients receiving intrathecal morphine remains controversial. This study evaluated the opioid-sparing efficacy of wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture as an adjunct to intrathecal morphine. METHODS: In this double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 188 patients undergoing elective caesarean delivery with intrathecal morphine (100 μg) received either wound infiltration with liposomal bupivacaine (266 mg) plus bupivacaine hydrochloride (100 mg), or saline placebo. All patients received standardised multimodal analgesia including scheduled non-opioid analgesics and hydromorphone patient-controlled analgesia. The primary outcome was cumulative opioid consumption (oral morphine milligram equivalents) at 48 h. RESULTS: With treatment, 48-h opioid consumption was significantly lower (12.60 mg [IQR 6.30-15.80] vs. 15.75 mg [IQR 9.45-25.50]; Hodges-Lehmann estimate -3.05 mg, 95% CI -5.9 to -1.4; P = 0.002). Secondary outcomes also favoured treatment: 24-h opioid consumption (6.30 vs. 9.45 mg; P < 0.001), movement-evoked pain at 24 h (40 vs. 50 mm; P < 0.001) and 48 h (30 vs. 40 mm; P < 0.001), time to first analgesic request (14.5 vs. 9.5 h; P < 0.001), and opioid-free status at 48 h (19.1% vs. 2.1%; RR 9.0; 95% CI 2.1-37.8; P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In women undergoing scheduled caesarean delivery, wound infiltration with a liposomal bupivacaine-bupivacaine hydrochloride admixture significantly reduced postoperative opioid consumption and improved pain scores. It may be an effective opioid-sparing adjunct to intrathecal morphine.

items.title: Pediatric Postoperative Acute Kidney Injury After Noncardiac Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) is associated with substantial morbidity and mortality. Reliable estimates of AKI after surgery in children are lacking. To address this gap, we aimed to synthesize the available evidence on the incidence of AKI after pediatric noncardiac surgery. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Cochrane and Web of Science for studies reporting the incidence of AKI, defined according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) criteria, within 7 postoperative days. Observational studies and clinical trials including patients aged < 18 years were eligible. The review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach. RESULTS: Twenty-seven studies (n = 21 908) were included. Considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 98.7%) and likely overrepresentation of clinically distinct high-risk populations limited the interpretability of a single overall pooled incidence estimate. The incidence was 22.3% (95% CI, 11.2-39.3) after neonatal surgery, 30.1% (95% CI, 21.4-40.6) after pediatric liver transplantation, and 9.2% (95% CI, 3.3-23.6) in mixed pediatric surgical populations. The certainty of evidence was rated low to very low. In mixed pediatric surgical populations, AKI incidence increased from 2.4% in American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) class 1-2 to 7.5% in ASA 3 (p < 0.001) and 18.9% in ASA 4-5 (p < 0.001), and decreased from 9.8% at 0-2 years to 4.0% at 12-18 years (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The reported incidence of postoperative AKI in children undergoing noncardiac surgery remains uncertain due to substantial heterogeneity and overrepresentation of high-risk populations. AKI incidence was high in neonates and liver transplant recipients and was associated with younger age and higher ASA class, although data were limited. Further prospective studies in broader pediatric surgical populations are needed to better assess the risk of postoperative AKI in children. TRIAL REGISTRATION: PROSPERO registration no.: CRD42024518832.

items.title: Pre-Extubation Low-Dose Propofol in Pediatric Ear, Nose, and Throat Procedures: A Meta-Analysis With Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Post-extubation emergence agitation (EA) is common in pediatric ear, nose, and throat (ENT) procedures and may lead to serious complications. AIMS: To assess the efficacy of low-dose propofol administered before extubation, compared with placebo, for preventing EA, using meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (TSA). METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing low-dose propofol versus placebo administered before extubation in pediatric ENT procedures. The primary outcomes were laryngospasm, severity of EA, assessed by the Pediatric Anesthesia Emergence Delirium (PAED) scale score, and incidence of EA. Secondary outcomes included post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) length of stay, time to recovery, and time to extubation. Random-effects models were used to pool effect estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). TSA was performed for all outcomes to assess the robustness of the evidence. RESULTS: Ten RCTs were included in the review, of which six (414 pediatric patients) contributed to the meta-analysis. Compared with control, propofol significantly reduced the incidence of EA (risk ratio [RR] = 0.57; 95% CI, 0.42-0.78) and lowered agitation severity (mean difference [MD] = -3.94; 95% CI, -5.74 to -2.13). Time to extubation was slightly longer (MD = 1.8 min; 95% CI, 1.4-2.3), whereas time to recovery (MD = 0.9 min; 95% CI, -1.9 to 3.6) and PACU length of stay (MD = -0.63 min; 95% CI, -3.2 to 1.9) did not differ. TSA confirmed the robustness of the findings for incidence of EA, severity of EA, and time to extubation. However, the certainty of evidence was very low for severity of EA and moderate for EA incidence and time to extubation. Laryngospasm outcomes were not pooled due to substantial heterogeneity. CONCLUSIONS: Our findings suggest that pre-extubation propofol probably reduces the incidence of EA in pediatric ENT surgery, supported by moderate-certainty evidence, and may lower EA severity measured by PAED scale scores, for which the certainty of evidence was very low. Propofol was also associated with a slightly longer time to extubation, with no difference in overall recovery time or PACU length of stay.

items.title: Effects of Esketamine on Emergence Delirium in Children Undergoing Sevoflurane Anesthesia: A Systematic Review, Meta-Analysis, and Trial Sequential Analysis.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Emergence delirium is a frequent and distressing postoperative complication in children, particularly following sevoflurane-based anesthesia. Despite its clinical importance, the optimal preventive strategy remains under investigation. This study aims to systematically evaluate the efficacy and safety of esketamine in preventing emergence delirium in pediatric patients undergoing sevoflurane-based general anesthesia. METHODS: We systematically searched seven databases and registries through 27 March 2026. Randomized controlled trials that compared esketamine with placebo in children undergoing surgical procedures were included. The primary outcome was the incidence of emergence delirium. Secondary outcomes were postoperative pain scores, extubation time, post-anesthesia care unit stay, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Data were synthesized using random-effects models, with risk ratios for dichotomous outcomes and mean differences or standardized mean differences for continuous outcomes. Meta-regression and trial sequential analysis were performed. The risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for randomized trials, and the certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation approach. RESULTS: Eight randomized controlled trials involving 916 patients were included. Esketamine significantly reduced the incidence of emergence delirium versus placebo (risk ratio = 0.35; 95% confidence interval: 0.26-0.48; p < 0.0001). No significant differences were observed between dosing regimens, surgical types, routes of administration, or timing of administration. Pain scores were significantly lower with esketamine (standardized mean difference = -0.58; 95% confidence interval: -0.79 to -0.37; p < 0.0001). Extubation time was modestly prolonged (mean difference = 1.72 min; 95% confidence interval: 0.20-3.24; p = 0.0267). Meta-regression revealed a statistically significant association between emergence delirium risk ratios and anesthesia duration (β = 0.98, p = 0.042), with no other significant associations observed for the other covariates. Post-anesthesia care unit stay showed no statistically significant difference, while postoperative nausea and vomiting was significantly reduced with esketamine (risk ratio = 0.69; 95% confidence interval: 0.49-0.97; p = 0.0304). items.title: Effect of Wrist Extension Angle on Radial and Ulnar Artery Sonoanatomy in Children: A Prospective Ultrasound Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Ultrasound-guided radial artery cannulation is common in pediatrics but technically challenging. While the ulnar artery is a potential alternative, its sonoanatomy relative to the radial artery is not well defined. AIMS: This study aimed to compare the sonoanatomic characteristics of the radial and ulnar arteries in children, evaluating how age, weight, and wrist position (0°, 30°, and 45°) influence arterial dimensions and depth to identify the most favorable profile for cannulation. METHODS: Ultrasound evaluation of the radial and ulnar arteries was performed at 0°, 30°, and 45° wrist extension in 180 anesthetized children aged 0-120 months using custom-made wooden blocks. Arterial dimensions and skin-to-artery distance were evaluated overall and across age (≤ 24 vs. > 24 months) and weight (≤ 12 vs. > 12 kg) subgroups to identify optimal access conditions. RESULTS: Wrist extension angle did not significantly affect anteroposterior diameter (1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.078), but significantly influenced transverse arterial diameter (1.5-1.6 mm, p = 0.003) and skin-to-artery distance (2.4-2.8 mm at 30°, p < 0.001). The radial artery was widest at 0° (1.6 ± 1.0 mm), while the ulnar artery peaked at 30° (1.6 ± 0.4 mm). Skin-to-artery distance was minimized at 30° for both vessels. In children ≤ 12 kg, radial transverse diameter decreased paradoxically from 0° to 45° (1.6 ± 0.4 to 1.4 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.013), while the ulnar artery was widest at 30° (1.5 ± 0.3 mm, p = 0.007). In infants ≤ 24 months, wrist angle did not significantly influence radial artery depth (p = 0.631, mean overall depth between 2.5-2.6 mm). CONCLUSION: A 30° wrist extension angle provides the most favorable sonoanatomic profile for both arteries. Although a larger vessel caliber may potentially facilitate cannulation, its clinical benefit remains uncertain as cannulation outcomes were not assessed. These findings support individualized ultrasound-guided assessment rather than a fixed positioning strategy.

items.title: Comparing Subglottic Ultrasound and Distal Phalanx Width for Pediatric Endotracheal Tube Sizing in a Predominantly School-Aged Pediatric Cohort: A Prospective Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accurate endotracheal tube (ETT) sizing is essential in pediatric airway management to optimize ventilation and reduce complications. Traditional methods, including age-based formulas and distal phalanx width (DPW), may lack precision. Subglottic ultrasound (US) has emerged as a promising tool, but its predictive accuracy compared with DPW remains unclear. This study aimed to compare accuracy, agreement, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of subglottic US versus DPW for predicting optimal ETT size in children, while recognizing that the enrolled cohort was predominantly school-aged. METHODS: In this prospective observational study, pediatric patients aged 0-12 years undergoing elective or emergency intubation were assessed. Pre-intubation measurements included subglottic transverse airway diameter by ultrasound (ACUSON Juniper, microconvex probe, 5-10 MHz) and DPW by digital calipers. Predicted ETT sizes were compared with the final clinically accepted cuffed ETT inner diameter confirmed by leak testing and cuff pressure optimization. Agreement was evaluated using Bland-Altman analysis and intraclass correlation coefficients, while diagnostic performance was defined a priori as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), likelihood ratios, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. Logistic regression identified predictors of good ETT fit. RESULTS: Among 160 patients, the median age was 8.8 years (IQR 7.0-10.5), indicating predominance of older children. Ultrasound-predicted ETT size showed a stronger correlation with actual size (r = 0.479, p < 0.001) than DPW (r = 0.248, p = 0.002). Ultrasound predictions had narrower Bland-Altman limits of agreement, although ultrasound measurement is operator-dependent. DPW showed poor sensitivity (5.9%) but high specificity (99.3%) for identifying underfit ETTs, with limited overall discrimination (ROC AUC = 0.53). Only subglottic diameter was a significant predictor of good ETT fit. CONCLUSION: Subglottic ultrasound showed better agreement with clinically accepted ETT size than DPW in this predominantly school-aged pediatric cohort. These findings support the potential role of ultrasound as an adjunct to pediatric airway assessment, but conclusions should be interpreted cautiously in infants and younger children because they were under-represented. Standardized measurement protocols and operator training are needed

items.title: Current Use, Monitoring and Reversal of Neuromuscular Block in Pediatric Anesthesia and Intensive Care: A Web-Based Cross-Sectional ESAIC Survey.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Neuromuscular blocking agents are recommended by the European Society of Anaesthesiology and Intensive Care (ESAIC) and European Society of Paediatric Anaesthesia (ESPA) for facilitating tracheal intubation in children. Despite these recommendations, real-world data on how neuromuscular blocking agents are used, monitored, and reversed remain scarce. AIMS: To identify and characterize self-reported neuromuscular blocking agent practice patterns across European and non-European countries, in the period preceding publication of the joint ESAIC and ESPA guidelines. METHODS: We conducted an anonymous, cross-sectional survey between 12 November and 12 December 2025, targeting members of the ESAIC, ESPA, and the French and Spanish national pediatric anesthesiology societies involved in pediatric airway management across 43 countries. RESULTS: The survey was accessed by 904 persons, and 874 responses were included in the analysis. Most participants were from Europe (83.5%) and worked in mixed pediatric anesthesia and intensive care settings (71.2%). Rocuronium was the most frequently used neuromuscular blocking agent for both routine tracheal intubation (68%; 95% CI 65%-71%) and rapid sequence intubation (67%; 95% CI 64%-70%). Neuromuscular blocking agents were used "always" or "mostly" before routine intubation in 47% of neonates (≤ 30 days) and 50% of infants (< 1 year), whereas "rarely" or "never" use was reported in 30% and 24%, respectively. Most respondents (56%) assessed adequacy of neuromuscular block using a fixed time interval after neuromuscular blocking agent administration. Reversal was administered "always" before extubation by 27% of respondents, while 9.3% reported "rarely" and 2.9% "never." Only half of participants used quantitative neuromuscular monitoring to guide reversal. Sugammadex was used by 47%. CONCLUSIONS: Self-reported clinical practice regarding neuromuscular blocking agent use in pediatric patients remains heterogeneous. Children are frequently intubated without neuromuscular blocking agents and extubated without consistent reversal. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring remains uncommon. These practice patterns raise concerns for patient safety.

items.title: Management of unintended dural puncture and postdural puncture headache in obstetrics: a narrative review.
items.abstract: Unintended dural puncture during epidural catheter placement for labor analgesia is uncommon but may result in postdural puncture headache, neurologic complications, psychological morbidity, and chronic head and back pain. This narrative review translates recent multisociety and intrathecal catheter guidelines, supplemented by contemporary observational and meta-analytic evidence, into practical point-of-care decision support for anesthesia clinicians. No procedural technique has been shown to reliably prevent unintended dural puncture. When it occurs, either performing a repeat epidural procedure or threading an intrathecal catheter may be appropriate; neither approach is clearly superior or reliably prevents postdural puncture headache. Safe management requires individualized pathway selection, cautious incremental neuraxial dosing, clear intrathecal or epidural catheter labeling, close hemodynamic monitoring, structured handover, and readiness to treat high or total spinal anesthesia. Current evidence does not support routine prophylactic epidural blood patch, prolonged intrathecal catheterization, or pharmacologic prophylaxis. Evaluation of postpartum headache should begin with screening for warning features and alternative diagnoses before postdural puncture headache is assumed. Conservative measures remain first-line treatment, whereas epidural blood patch is appropriate for moderate-to-severe or refractory symptoms, symptoms that limit daily activities, or when neurologic features are present. Because postdural puncture headache is associated with serious neurologic and psychological morbidity and chronic pain, care should include written discharge instructions, defined follow-up until symptom resolution, communication with primary care clinicians, and prompt imaging or specialist referral when symptoms are atypical, progressive, or refractory.

items.title: The role of central nervous system sensitization in obstetric pain: A focused review.
items.abstract: Obstetric pain conditions are clinically significant but often underrecognized complications of pregnancy and childbirth. Central nervous system sensitization (central sensitization) refers to the amplification of neural signaling in the central nervous system leading to pain hypersensitivity and offers a mechanistic framework for understanding acute and persistent obstetric pain. Central sensitization does not, however, act in isolation. It is initiated and sustained by ongoing input from sensitized peripheral nociceptors, potentially associated with pain amplification and persistence. This focused review synthesizes the neurophysiological mechanisms which may underlie sensitization in the peripartum period and examines the main obstetric pain conditions in which sensitization has been implicated, including pregnancy-related lumbopelvic pain, labor pain and persistent postpartum pain after vaginal delivery, persistent perineal pain, and chronic postcesarean pain. We also discuss psychological factors including anxiety, depression, pain catastrophizing, and fear of childbirth, as potential active modulators of central pain processing rather than merely coexisting conditions. These factors may represent modifiable targets for prevention, mitigation, and management. Key evidence gaps include the absence of obstetric-specific validation for clinical assessment tools such as the Central Sensitization Inventory, and limited prospective data linking intraprocedural nociception to postprocedural pain sensitization. Addressing these gaps through rigorously designed peripartum studies is essential for developing targeted, mechanism-based strategies to prevent and treat obstetric pain.

items.title: Oral calcium intake during labor in healthy women: a pharmacokinetic study.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Recent studies suggest that intravenous calcium may reduce postpartum hemorrhage due to uterine atony. However, intravenous lines may be unavailable in low-resource settings. We thus evaluated the time course of change in serum ionized calcium after pregnant women ingested commonly available oral calcium formulations. METHODS: Term, laboring patients 18-45 years of age received oral calcium carbonate (1200 mg). Blood samples were obtained to measure ionized calcium before and after ingestion. Following interim analysis demonstrating minimal effect, the protocol was amended to calcium citrate (1250 mg). Enrollment was stopped at 20 of 60 planned participants for futility without a prespecified statistical futility boundary. RESULTS: We observed minimal to no increase in serum ionized calcium in ten patients who received calcium carbonate and eight patients who received calcium citrate. CONCLUSION: The package insert-recommended dose of two oral calcium formulations failed to meaningfully increase serum ionized calcium in laboring patients. Future studies should center on intravenous calcium until alternative oral calcium dosing or formulations successfully increase maternal ionized calcium.

items.title: CoolStick vs. ethyl chloride spray for sensory block testing to light touch and cold for caesarean delivery under neuraxial anaesthesia: a paired method-comparison study with randomised test order.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Light touch sensation is recommended when testing neuraxial anaesthesia for caesarean delivery. This is commonly assessed using ethyl chloride spray. CoolStick is a more environmentally sustainable device that has not been compared to conventional methods. METHODS: This was a multicentre prospective paired method-comparison study with randomised test order involving participants undergoing planned caesarean delivery with spinal or combined spinal-epidural anaesthesia. Participants were tested with both CoolStick and ethyl chloride 10 min post-spinal, with the initial method chosen at random. The primary endpoint was dermatomal level to light touch, and the secondary endpoint was dermatomal level to cold. We also assessed pain within 60 min of spinal injection. Agreement between testing methods was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient, with bias and limits of agreement assessed using Bland-Altman plots and the Wilcoxon signed rank test. RESULTS: We recruited 64 women between April and November 2025. The median [interquartile range] age was 34 (30-37) years. The intraclass correlation coefficient for light touch was 0.87 (95% CI 0.78-0.92, P < 0.001), and for cold was 0.89 (95% CI 0.83-0.93, P < 0.001). Median bias for light touch was 0 dermatomes (95% limits of agreement -1 to 4, p = 0.002) and for cold was 0 dermatomes (-2 to 1, P = 0.06). No patient reported pain within 60 min. DISCUSSION: We found high overall agreement between devices for both light touch and cold testing. However, CoolStick recorded light touch levels several dermatomes lower than ethyl chloride in a small proportion of patients.

items.title: Perioperative Outcomes in Stage 1 Palliated Infants Undergoing Noncardiac Procedures: A Comparison by Shunt Type.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Interstage infants with single-ventricle (SV) physiology following Stage I palliation represent a high-risk population for noncardiac procedures requiring anesthesia. Data comparing perioperative outcomes by shunt type remain limited. AIMS: Describe anesthetic management, perioperative complications, and postoperative outcomes in interstage SV infants undergoing noncardiac interventions and compare outcomes between right ventricle-to-pulmonary artery (Sano) and modified Blalock-Taussig-Thomas shunt (mBTTS) patients. METHODS: We performed a retrospective single-center cohort study of interstage SV infants with Stage I palliation undergoing noncardiac surgery or nonsurgical procedures requiring anesthesia between 2015 and 2023. Outcomes were stratified by shunt type. RESULTS: A total of 208 noncardiac interventions in 120 interstage SV infants were analyzed; 136 (65.4%) encounters in 86 Sano patients and 72 (34.6%) encounters in 34 mBTTS patients. Compared with mBTTS infants, Sano patients underwent interventions at a younger age (57 [IQR 40-83] vs. 105 [59-278] days, p < 0.001) and lower weight (3.6 [3.0-4.1] vs. 4.8 [3.4-7.3] kg, p < 0.001). mBTTS procedures had higher rates of ventricular dysfunction (34.3% vs. 12.7%, p < 0.001), chromosomal abnormalities (63.9% vs. 19.1%, p < 0.001), gastrointestinal comorbidities (87.5% vs. 72.1%, p = 0.014), and hematologic comorbidities (41.7% vs. 22.8%, p = 0.006). Hemodynamic instability requiring vasoactive support was the most common perioperative complication and occurred similarly between groups (31.9% mBTTS vs. 31.6% Sano, p = 0.962). There were no perioperative cardiac arrests. Rates of postoperative escalation of care (2.9%), reintubation (3.0% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999), readmission (16.2% vs. 16.9%, p = 0.999), and 30-day mortality (2.3% vs. 2.9%, p = 0.999) were low and comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Despite the high-risk physiology of interstage SV patients, perioperative outcomes were comparable between Sano and mBTTS cohorts. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and should not imply low procedural risk. Favorable outcomes likely reflect careful patient selection, multidisciplinary perioperative care, and specialized institutional expertise.

items.title: Association between early sensory level following spinal anesthesia and intraoperative pain during cesarean delivery: a retrospective cohort study (2019-2020).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Spinal anesthesia is widely used for cesarean delivery; however, some patients experience intraoperative pain or discomfort. This study investigated the association between early onset with rapid cephalad spread of spinal anesthesia and intraoperative pain during cesarean delivery. METHODS: In this retrospective study conducted at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, a total of 427 cesarean deliveries were evaluated. Data on sensory block levels at 5 and 10 min after intrathecal injection were extracted from anesthesia records. Intraoperative pain was defined as a distressing sensation managed with supplemental analgesia. Multivariable logistic regression models evaluated associations of sensory block levels at 5 and 10 min with intraoperative pain. RESULTS: Pain occurred in 56 patients (13.1%). Among patients experiencing intraoperative pain, the mean sensory level was lower compared with patients without pain at 5 min (8.1 ± 1.8 vs 6.8 ± 1.9; mean difference, 1.3 dermatomes; P < 0.001) and at 10 min (5.8 ± 1.6 vs 4.7 ± 1.2, mean difference, 1.1 dermatomes; P < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression models, each 1-dermatome lower sensory level at 5 min was associated with 16% higher adjusted odds of intraoperative pain (aOR, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.01-1.33; P = 0.035), while at 10 min, it was associated with 43% higher odds (aOR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.18-1.74; P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Lower sensory levels during the first 10 min after intrathecal injection were associated with pain, despite an apparently adequate T4 sensory block at skin incision, suggesting that slower onset might predict intraoperative pain during cesarean delivery.

items.title: Risk factors for positive depression screening at 6 weeks postpartum: a single center retrospective cohort study (2014-2023).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: As universal postpartum depression screening is implemented, contemporary risk factors for positive screens in the United States population remain understudied. Our aim was to evaluate demographic, obstetric, neonatal, anesthetic and psychiatric factors associated with positive depression screening scores at 6 weeks postpartum. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at an academic center in the United States (2014-2023). Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale scores recorded at 6 weeks postpartum were analyzed (positive screen score ≥ 10). We included adults (≥18 years) delivering a live or nonviable fetus from gestational age ≥ 20 weeks by any mode who completed screening at 6 weeks post-delivery; we excluded patients with an incomplete or missing score. The primary outcome was factors independently associated with a positive depression screen at 6 weeks postpartum. Secondary outcomes were to characterize depression scores and explore differences in inpatient pain outcomes based on positive or negative depression screening at 6 weeks postpartum. RESULTS: Of 8155 deliveries analyzed, 13.6% (n = 1107) screened positive on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale. Factors independently associated with higher odds of a positive screen included Hispanic ethnicity, single marital status, delivery of neonate with very low birth weight, worst postpartum pain score up to 48 h following delivery, and psychiatric diagnosis. Positive and negative screen median scores were 12 [IQR 11-16] {Range 10-27} and 3 [IQR 1-5] {Range 0-9}, respectively. The positive depression screening group experienced worse inpatient pain. CONCLUSION: Future studies should explore inpatient pain as a potential predictor of positive 6-week depression screening.

items.title: Quadratus lumborum block with or without subfascial wound catheter and post-caesarean delivery pain outcomes: a single-center retrospective cohort study (2026).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: We evaluated whether adding a subfascial wound catheter to a posterior quadratus lumborum block-based multimodal analgesic pathway improves pain and recovery after caesarean delivery. METHODS: This retrospective cohort included 361 women undergoing scheduled or urgent caesarean delivery from January to June 2026. All received bilateral posterior quadratus lumborum block and non-opioid multimodal analgesia; wound catheter use was optional. Ropivacaine infusion was continued for 48 h. Pain scores were recorded at 6, 24, and 48 h. Mobilisation, rescue analgesia, satisfaction, breastfeeding-related concern, breastfeeding outcomes, and repeat quadratus lumborum block were assessed. Catheter effects on pain were analysed using generalized estimating equations adjusted for anaesthetic technique, operative duration, repeat caesarean delivery, adhesions, age, and blood loss. RESULTS: Catheter use was associated with lower pain scores at 6 h (adjusted difference - 0.209, 95% confidence interval - 0.369 to -0.049; P = 0.011) and 24 h (-0.174, -0.309 to -0.039; P = 0.012), but not at 48 h (-0.016, -0.139 to 0.108; P = 0.805). These differences were too small to be clinically meaningful. Mobilisation, rescue analgesia, satisfaction, and breastfeeding outcomes were similar between groups. Breastfeeding-related concern was greater with catheter use. Repeat quadratus lumborum block was infrequently required and did not delay return to normal activity. DISCUSSION: Subfascial wound catheter use was not associated with clinically meaningful additional pain or recovery benefit. Patient counselling may help address breastfeeding-related concerns.

items.title: Impact of the infusion line on co-loading and highly diluted norepinephrine administration through a single peripheral venous catheter: An in vitro simulation of the infusion protocol used during cesarean delivery under spinal anesthesia.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid crystalloid co-loading and prophylactic norepinephrine may share a peripheral intravenous catheter during cesarean delivery. We assessed whether infusion-system architecture alters fluid and drug delivery. METHODS: Six infusion-system configurations were tested in vitro. Norepinephrine 8 μg/mL was infused at 30 mL/h (4 μg/min) while 1000 mL saline was delivered from a pressure bag initially inflated to 300 mmHg. Outcomes were crystalloid volume delivered during the first 10 min, time within the norepinephrine target range of 3.5-4.5 μg/min, and the proportion of measurements outside ±12.5% of the configuration-specific median. RESULTS: Crystalloid volume at 10 min ranged from 596 ± 30 to 947 ± 30 mL between configurations (P < 0.001). Time within the norepinephrine target range ranged from 32.8 ± 6.1% to 71.4 ± 9.9% (P = 0.019), and instability ranged from 23.8 ± 6.2% to 54.6 ± 13.0% (P < 0.001). Among the configurations tested, those in which pressurized crystalloid entered downstream of the convergence of actively controlled drug infusions showed the most favorable balance between crystalloid delivery and norepinephrine stability. DISCUSSION: Infusion-system architecture influenced both rapid crystalloid delivery and distal norepinephrine stability. When pressurized crystalloid and actively controlled drugs share a peripheral intravenous catheter, a distal crystalloid entry may represent a favorable system architecture. Clinical relevance requires further evaluation.

items.title: Antepartum obstructive sleep apnea screening and its association with postpartum respiratory depression: a retrospective cohort study (2020-2025).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obstructive sleep apnea is not routinely screened for in the peripartum population, and its association with postpartum respiratory depression remains unclear. We evaluated positive antepartum obstructive sleep apnea screening and its association with postpartum respiratory outcomes. METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of parturients undergoing routine antepartum obstructive sleep apnea STOP screening (loud snoring, daytime tiredness, observed apnea, high blood pressure) from July 2020 to June 2025. Delivery encounters with at least one STOP response were included. Positive STOP screening was defined as ≥2 criteria. Postpartum respiratory outcomes included bradypnea, oxygen desaturation, and naloxone administration. Associations of positive STOP screening, individual STOP components, and self-reported obstructive sleep apnea with postpartum respiratory outcomes were evaluated using logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 19,250 delivery encounters, 608 (3.2%) screened positive and 182 (1.0%) reported obstructive sleep apnea. Bradypnea occurred in 2.8% (532/19,237) and oxygen desaturation in 2.4% (356/14,723). Positive STOP screening was associated with desaturation (adjusted OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.21-2.88; P = 0.005), but not bradypnea. Preeclampsia or a hypertensive diagnosis was associated with bradypnea (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.14-2.35) and desaturation (OR 2.88, 95% CI 2.06-4.03). Self-reported obstructive sleep apnea was associated with bradypnea (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.06-3.84) and desaturation (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.46-5.08). Snoring, tiredness, and observed apnea were associated with desaturation but not bradypnea. CONCLUSION: Positive antepartum STOP screening was associated with postpartum desaturation but not bradypnea. Preeclampsia or a hypertensive diagnosis may be an important screening question for postpartum respiratory depression.

items.title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia for Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Postoperative Cognitive Phenotype.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. METHODS: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9 to 11 yr, with or without previous general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. RESULTS: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (chi-square[1] = 0.01; P = 0.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure, 4.47 ± 3.00 yr) and nonexposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: efficient and vulnerable executive control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with slightly higher odds of belonging to the vulnerable profile group (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI; 1.151 to 1.159; P < 0.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, general anesthesia-exposed participants showed higher global-local precedence measures (estimate, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.04 to 1.01; P = 0.036). CONCLUSIONS: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential postoperative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a higher likelihood to belonging to a vulnerable executive control profile, together with greater visuo-spatial global-local precedence.

items.title: Complications in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation: an analysis of the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Difficult tracheal intubation is associated with serious complications, including hypoxia, bradycardia and cardiac arrest. Neonates have increased physiologic vulnerability compared with older children, yet detailed data on management strategies and outcomes in neonates with difficult tracheal intubation remain limited. We hypothesised that clinicians have lower first-attempt tracheal intubation success and higher complication rates for neonates compared with older children with difficult tracheal intubation. METHODS: We analysed the Pediatric Difficult Intubation Registry to determine tracheal intubation first attempt success and incidence of complications. We used logistic regression to identify variables associated with complications in neonates. RESULTS: During the study period, 6283 paediatric difficult tracheal intubations were recorded, including 420 neonates. First attempt success was lower for neonates (139/420, 33.1%) than older children (2394/4683, 51.1%). Complications occurred more frequently in neonates (123/420, 29.3%) than older children (637/4683, 13.6%). Hypoxia occurred in 92/420 (21.9%) neonates and 269/4683 (5.7%) older children. Severe complications were more frequent in neonates vs. older children (12/420, 2.9% vs. 30/4683, 0.6%, respectively), with cardiac arrests occurring in 4/420 (1.0%) neonates and 11/4683 (0.2%) older children. Difficult mask ventilation occurred more frequently in neonates (60/420, 14.3%) than older children (353/4681, 7.5%). In neonates, increased number of tracheal intubation attempts (aOR 1.61 per attempt, 95%CI 1.30-2.00, p < 0.001) and difficult facemask ventilation (aOR 3.17, 95%CI 1.38-7.30, p = 0.007) were associated with complications. Anticipated difficulty with airway management had a protective effect (aOR 0.37, 95%CI 0.16-0.88, p = 0.025). DISCUSSION: Neonates with difficult tracheal intubation experience a substantially higher rate of complications than older children. Early recognition of risk is critical in order to enable careful planning to minimise tracheal intubation attempts in this vulnerable population. We compared how often the tube was placed successfully on the first try and how often problems occurred in newborn babies and older children. items.title: Effects of Different Measures for the Treatment of Arterial Hypotension on Cerebral Oxygen Saturation During Pediatric General Anesthesia: An Observational Pilot Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intraoperative hypotension is a common complication in pediatric anesthesia. The definition of hypotension and treatment strategies are heterogeneous. The association of these treatments with cerebral regional oxygen saturation, measured by near-infrared spectroscopy, is insufficiently characterized. AIMS: The study explores whether changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate differ after the administration of an isotonic fluid bolus, noradrenaline, adrenaline, or cafedrine/theodrenaline for perioperative hypotension in children. METHODS: This single-center, observational pilot study included children aged 18 years or younger undergoing noncardiac surgery who developed hypotension requiring treatment. The choice of the intervention was at the discretion of the attending anesthetist and guided by an internal guideline. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation, mean arterial pressure, and heart rate were recorded for 8 min after the first intervention and analyzed relative to the value immediately before treatment. Groups were compared using the area under the curve of these changes and linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: Forty-six patients were analyzed. Cerebral regional oxygen saturation immediately before treatment did not differ from the pre-induction baseline. Cafedrine/theodrenaline was the only treatment associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, with a significantly higher area under the curve than noradrenaline (p = 0.017), adrenaline (p = 0.017), and fluid administration (p < 0.001), which was confirmed by mixed-effects models. Only cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with an increase in heart rate. Changes in heart rate were significantly correlated with changes in cerebral regional oxygen saturation (Spearman's ρ = 0.376, p = 0.010), but not with changes in mean arterial pressure. CONCLUSIONS: Cafedrine/theodrenaline was associated with a sustained increase in cerebral regional oxygen saturation, heart rate, and blood pressure. Noradrenaline, adrenaline, and fluid administration were associated with unchanged or decreasing cerebral regional oxygen saturation. Randomized controlled studies are required to confirm these findings.

items.title: Ultrasound-Guided Supraclavicular Brachiocephalic Vein Cannulation in Pediatric Patients With Hematological Disorders: A Retrospective Comparative Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Central venous access is indispensable for clinical management of pediatric patients with hematological disorders, including chemotherapy administration, blood product transfusion, and critical rescue. Repeated venipuncture attempts, procedural failure, postoperative catheter malposition, and cannulation-related complications can substantially disrupt subsequent treatment courses and compromise therapeutic efficacy. AIMS: This retrospective study aimed to evaluate the feasibility and safety of ultrasound-guided brachiocephalic vein (BCV) cannulation, with the goal of optimizing central venous catheterization protocols, reducing procedure-related adverse events, and improving the efficiency and safety of treatment via central venous access in pediatric patients. METHODS: This retrospective study included 580 children (303 subclavian vein [SCV], 277 BCV) who underwent ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization between January 2021 and December 2024. We compared first-attempt success rate, overall success rate, procedural duration, intraoperative adverse events, postoperative complications, and catheter malposition. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was used to improve comparability between the groups with respect to measured baseline covariates. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent risk factors. RESULTS: After IPTW, the BCV approach was associated with a higher first-attempt success rate (OR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.05-2.81; risk difference [RD] = 0.119, 95% CI: 0.015-0.222) and a higher overall success rate (RD = 0.091, 95% CI: 0.013-0.168). The mean procedural duration was 6 min shorter in the BCV group (95% CI: -9.5 to -2.5). The BCV approach was independently associated with lower odds of intraoperative malposition (OR = 0.096, 95% CI: 0.037-0.249), postoperative malposition (OR = 0.34, 95% CI: 0.16-0.74), and perioperative complications (OR = 0.28, 95% CI: 0.08-0.94). Multivariable regression analysis showed that catheterization approach was independently associated with catheter malposition. CONCLUSIONS: Compared with SCV, ultrasound-guided BCV cannulation is associated with higher success rates, shorter procedural duration, and fewer malpositions and complications. This technique may offer particular benefits for children with hematological disorders.

items.title: Psychometric Evaluation of the Turkish Version of the Induction Compliance Checklist in Children Undergoing Mask Anesthesia.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Many children undergoing anesthesia commonly exhibit distress behaviors such as anxiety, crying, and physical resistance. Assessment of this behavior is important as it could lead to postoperative behavioral changes and delayed recovery. AIM: The aim of this study was to evaluate the content validity, construct validity, internal consistency, and inter-observer reliability of the Turkish version of the Induction Compliance Checklist (ICC), which was developed to assess compliance behaviors in children during anesthesia induction. METHODS: The study was planned as a prospective observational study. Following translation of the original ICC, content validity was examined using the Davis technique with the opinions of 10 experts. Next, Turkish ICC was applied simultaneously and independently by three independent observers during mask induction to 184 children (ASA I-III) aged 1-7 years undergoing anesthesia and surgery. Inter-observer reliability was evaluated with Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) and Fleiss Kappa/Gwet's AC1; internal consistency with KR-20 and McDonald's omega; and construct validity with single-factor confirmatory factor analysis (WLSMV). Item analysis was performed with a tetrachoric correlation matrix, floor and ceiling effects. RESULTS: Content validity was excellent (I-CVI 0.90-1.00, S-CVI≈0.99). Inter-observer reliability for the total score was excellent: InCC (1, 2) = 0.92 (95% CI: 0.90-0.94), InCC (2, 3) = 0.97 (95% CI: 0.96-0.98). At the item level, Gwet's AC1 values ranged from 0.81 to 0.97, while Kappa values were generally 0.75-0.90 except for M11. Internal consistency was at an acceptable level with KR-20 0.49-0.52 and McDonald's omega 0.66-0.82. These results are low due to the floor effect caused by premedication. Confirmatory factor analysis moderately supported the single-factor structure (best fit in Observer Surgeon: CFI = 0.927, TLI = 0.907). High floor effect was prominent especially in rarely observed severe behaviors (M7-M11); strong correlation was observed between M9-M10 (0.89-0.94). CONCLUSIONS: Following rigorous analysis, we found that the Turkish ICC is a reliable and valid tool that can assess children's compliance behaviors during pediatric anesthesia induction. Excellent inter-observer agreement and high content validity support its suitability for clinical and research use.
